# Introduction

I wanted to work on recommendation for this project because it's a
genuinely different kind of machine-learning problem from anything else
in my usual toolkit. Most tabular projects are supervised: there's a `y`
the model is trying to predict, and a metric that scores how close its
predictions come. Recommendation doesn't have that — there's no single
"correct" next item — and once I started reading around the topic, I
realized it splits into two genuinely different techniques depending on
what data happens to be available:

- **Content-based** — no user data needed at all. Compare items by their
  own measurable properties (here, Spotify's audio features) and
  recommend whatever's most similar.
- **Collaborative filtering** — no item content needed at all. Learn
  from real user/item interaction history (here, KKBox's listening
  logs) instead.

Rather than pick one, I built and evaluated one working system of each
kind, then put them side by side. That wasn't to crown a winner — they
solve different problems, with different data requirements, so "which
one wins" isn't really a coherent question to ask across both. I did it
because comparing how each is built, evaluated, and interpreted taught
me more about what recommendation actually is than building either one
in isolation would have.

# Part I — Content-Based Recommendation (Spotify)

The question I set out to answer here: given a track someone likes, can
I recommend other tracks whose *audio* resembles it — not tracks other,
similar listeners happened to play, since there's no listener data in
this dataset at all. Every recommendation comes from Spotify's own
audio-feature measurements: danceability, energy, acousticness, and so
on. I built this on Kaggle's [Spotify Tracks
Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/maharshipandya/-spotify-tracks-dataset).

## Data

~114,000 tracks, roughly 1,000 sampled per genre across 114 genres, each
with:

- **Audio features** (Spotify's own per-track measurements):
  `danceability`, `energy`, `loudness`, `speechiness`, `acousticness`,
  `instrumentalness`, `liveness`, `valence` (musical positivity), `tempo`,
  `key` (one of 12 pitch classes), `mode` (major/minor), `time_signature`.
- **Metadata**: `track_name`, `artists`, `album_name`, `duration_ms`,
  `explicit`.
- **`popularity`** — a Spotify-computed score, and **`track_genre`** — a
  human-assigned genre tag. Neither is used as a recommender *input*
  feature (see Methodology) — both are reserved for evaluation.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based import config, data

tracks_df = data.load_tracks()
print(f"{len(tracks_df)} tracks, {tracks_df[config.GENRE_COL].nunique()} genres")
tracks_df[config.RAW_AUDIO_NUMERIC_COLS + [config.GENRE_COL, config.POPULARITY_COL]].describe(include="all").T
```

### Why I excluded `popularity` and `track_genre` from the feature space

I was tempted to throw every available column into the feature space
and let the model sort it out, but two of them would have quietly broken
the whole exercise. Including `popularity` as a recommendation feature
would make the system chase what's already trending rather than what
actually sounds similar — the opposite of a useful recommender.
Including `track_genre` directly would make the genre-matching
evaluation below trivially easy (the recommender would just be reading
the answer off the genre column), which would prove nothing about
whether the *audio* similarity is meaningful. So I kept both out of the
feature space entirely and only bring them back afterward, to score
results.

## Feature engineering

I engineered three features, detailed in
`src/recommendation_showcase/content_based/features.py`:

- **`key_sin` / `key_cos`** — my first instinct was to leave `key` as a
  plain integer, until I remembered it's actually 12 pitch classes
  arranged in a circle: key 11 is one semitone from key 0, not "far
  away" from it the way a plain integer or a flat one-hot encoding would
  imply. Encoding it as a point on a circle (sine and cosine of the
  angle) preserves that adjacency — the standard trick for any cyclical
  feature, and the same idea I'd reach for with week-of-year or
  hour-of-day.
- **`duration_min`** — `duration_ms / 60000`, a pure readability
  transform, nothing more.
- **`mood_quadrant`** — buckets each track into one of four moods
  (energetic/calm x happy/dark) from Russell's circumplex model of
  affect, using training-data medians of `valence`/`energy` as the
  quadrant boundaries. The classifier can already learn this distinction
  from the raw floats directly, so this feature doesn't add predictive
  power — I added it purely for human legibility in the notebook and
  app, where "energetic_happy" reads far more naturally than two
  decimals.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based.features import FeatureEngineer

sample = tracks_df.sample(3000, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED)
engineered = FeatureEngineer().fit_transform(sample)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
sns.scatterplot(data=engineered, x="valence", y="energy", hue="mood_quadrant", alpha=0.5, ax=ax, palette=PALETTE[:4])
ax.set_title("Every sampled track's (valence, energy), colored by mood_quadrant")
plt.show()
```

The four color clusters aren't perfectly separated blobs — they shade
into each other near the median cutoffs, which makes sense since mood is
genuinely continuous, not four discrete buckets. What this chart tells
me is that the quadrant labels are a reasonable simplification for
reading a chart or scanning a recommendation list, but the actual
distance calculations underneath still use the raw `valence`/`energy`
floats, not this coarser summary.

## Methodology

### The recommender: weighted nearest-neighbor search

`ContentRecommender` (`content_based/model.py`) standardizes every audio
feature first — scale matters directly for distance in a way it never
would for a tree-based model, since a raw feature with a wide numeric
range (like `loudness`, roughly -60 to 0) would otherwise dominate the
distance calculation over a feature that's actually more musically
meaningful but happens to live on a 0-1 scale (like `danceability`).
After scaling, it finds the `k` nearest tracks by Euclidean distance in
that feature space. I tried three optional ways to reshape that distance
metric before the search runs, and evaluated each below rather than
assuming any of them would help:

- **Importance-weighted** — fit a genre classifier on the same features
  and use its learned feature importances to *weight* the distance
  metric: a feature the classifier leans on to separate genres counts
  more toward "closeness."
- **PCA** — project onto the top 10 principal components before
  searching. With only ~25 features to begin with, this is more a test
  of whether discarding lower-variance components denoises the space
  than a genuine dimensionality-curse fix (PCA's usual selling point
  matters more at hundreds or thousands of dimensions than it does here).
- **NCA** (Neighborhood Components Analysis) — learn a linear projection
  via gradient descent that directly maximizes KNN accuracy under the
  genre labels, a metric *learned specifically for* nearest-neighbor
  search rather than borrowed from elsewhere. Its cost scales roughly
  quadratically with row count and gets OOM-killed on this project's
  full ~72k-row training split (I verified this directly — the process
  gets killed by the OS for exhausting memory), so it's fit on a
  5,000-row subsample instead, then applied to the full catalog.

### Evaluating a recommender with no user-feedback data: precision@k

There's no click-through or replay data here, so I needed a different
way to check whether the recommendations are any good. I used
**precision@k**: hold out a set of tracks, recommend `k` tracks for each
from the remaining catalog, and measure what fraction of those
recommendations share the query track's true genre. Genre is an
imperfect proxy for "actually sounds alike" — two tracks in different
genres can sound more similar than two tracks stuck with the same label
— but it's the standard fallback when no real feedback signal exists,
and it's measurable, which is what I actually need here.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based import model

train_df, test_df = model.train_test_split_tracks(tracks_df, test_size=0.2)

X_train, y_train = data.split_features_target(train_df)
classifier_pipeline = model.build_classifier_pipeline(model.random_forest_estimator())
classifier_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
weights = model.compute_feature_weights_from_classifier(classifier_pipeline)

results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"approach": "Popularity baseline", "precision_at_10": model.popularity_baseline_precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10)},
    {"approach": "Unweighted KNN", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10)},
    {"approach": "Importance-weighted KNN", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, feature_weights=weights)},
    {"approach": "PCA(10) KNN", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, embedding=model.pca_embedding(10))},
    {
        "approach": "NCA(10) KNN",
        "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(
            train_df, test_df, k=10, embedding=model.nca_embedding(10), embedding_fit_sample_size=5000
        ),
    },
])
results
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.barh(results["approach"], results["precision_at_10"], color=[PALETTE[3], PALETTE[2], PALETTE[0], PALETTE[1], PALETTE[4]])
ax.set_xlabel("Precision@10")
plt.show()
```

This chart is the payoff of the whole evaluation exercise: every method
beats the popularity baseline by a wide margin, which tells me the audio
features genuinely carry usable genre signal rather than noise.
Importance-weighted KNN came out on top of the five — the more
"principled" methods (PCA, NCA) didn't beat this simpler heuristic here,
which genuinely surprised me going in, since NCA is literally optimizing
for the metric being measured. That's a result only knowable by
measuring it directly, not by assuming a fancier-sounding technique
automatically wins — PCA barely moved the needle (consistent with there
being little redundancy to remove in only ~25 features), and NCA
improved on plain KNN but still fell short of the importance-weighted
approach, plausibly handicapped by having to learn its projection from a
5,000-row subsample rather than the full catalog.

### Is exact-genre matching too strict?

Something about the precision@10 numbers above bothered me, so I
checked it directly: several of this dataset's 113 genre tags turned
out to be near-synonyms applied to the *same physical track* — 24,259 of
the raw 114,000 rows are exact-duplicate `track_id`s carrying a
different genre tag each time. That means exact-genre precision@k
counts a recommendation landing on a near-synonym as a complete miss,
which felt like it might be understating how good the recommender
actually is. `genre_families.py` groups the 113 tags into 13 broader
families (plus a `mood_context` bucket for tags like `chill`/`sad`/
`study` that are playlist moods, not musical genres) so I could see how
much of that gap is really just near-synonym mismatches.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based.genre_families import GENRE_TO_FAMILY

granularity = pd.DataFrame([
    {"approach": "Popularity baseline", "granularity": "Exact genre", "precision_at_10": model.popularity_baseline_precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10)},
    {"approach": "Popularity baseline", "granularity": "Genre family", "precision_at_10": model.popularity_baseline_precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, genre_map=GENRE_TO_FAMILY)},
    {"approach": "Importance-weighted KNN", "granularity": "Exact genre", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, feature_weights=weights)},
    {"approach": "Importance-weighted KNN", "granularity": "Genre family", "precision_at_10": model.precision_at_k(train_df, test_df, k=10, feature_weights=weights, genre_map=GENRE_TO_FAMILY)},
])
granularity.pivot(index="approach", columns="granularity", values="precision_at_10")
```

My first reaction to this table was that the ~14x jump in the
popularity baseline's score might undercut the earlier result — but
working through the ratios reassured me. The popularity baseline jumps
~14x at the looser genre-family granularity, while the recommender only
roughly doubles — so the recommender's advantage over the naive baseline
is actually *larger* in relative terms at the strict exact-genre level
(~18x) than at the family level (~2.7x). Coarser bins flatter every
method's absolute score, including pure guessing, which is exactly why a
bigger number at the family level isn't the more honest one to lead
with. What holds up across both framings — and what I actually care
about — is that the recommender clearly and consistently beats the
baseline either way, just by a different margin depending on how
strictly "correct" is defined.

## Interpretability: what separates genres?

The genre classifier exists specifically to produce the importance
weights above and to be explained — not to be a high-scoring classifier
in its own right (114 genres is a genuinely hard multiclass problem, and
I didn't expect it to score well as a classifier on its own terms). I
used **SHAP** (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to see which features it
actually leans on, rather than take the feature-importance weights on
faith.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.content_based.interpretability import compute_shap_values, top_shap_features

explanation, _ = compute_shap_values(classifier_pipeline, X_train, max_samples=500)
top = top_shap_features(explanation, top_n=10).sort_values("mean_abs_shap")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5))
ax.barh(top["feature"], top["mean_abs_shap"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value|")
ax.set_title("Top 10 features distinguishing genres")
plt.show()
```

`instrumentalness` and `acousticness` come out on top, ahead of
`danceability` and `duration_min`. That lines up with how I'd describe
genres myself — "acoustic" vs. "electronic," "instrumental" vs.
"vocal-heavy" are some of the first things I'd listen for — which gives
me some confidence that the classifier (and by extension the
importance-weighted distance metric it feeds) is picking up on
musically real distinctions, not some quirk of the data.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Captured for the head-to-head comparison later in this report.
cb_best_precision_exact = results.set_index("approach").loc["Importance-weighted KNN", "precision_at_10"]
cb_best_precision_family = granularity.set_index(["approach", "granularity"]).loc[
    ("Importance-weighted KNN", "Genre family"), "precision_at_10"
]
cb_baseline_precision = results.set_index("approach").loc["Popularity baseline", "precision_at_10"]
```

# Part II — Collaborative Filtering (KKBox)

For the second half of this project I wanted to try the other kind of
recommendation problem — one built entirely on real user behavior
instead of item properties. The task: given a real member's listening
history and a specific song, predict whether they'll listen to it again
within a month of first hearing it. I built this on Kaggle's real [WSDM
— KKBox's Music Recommendation
Challenge](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kkbox-music-recommendation-challenge)
(2018). Unlike Part I, this needs no audio content at all — the whole
task is defined by real user/song interaction history — and it's scored
by AUC on a real Kaggle leaderboard, which meant I could check my
results against a public benchmark rather than just my own intuition.

## Data

Four tables, verified directly against the real downloaded files:

- **`train.csv`/`test.csv`** (7,377,418 / 2,556,791 rows): one row per
  listening event — `msno` (member), `song_id`, three context columns
  (`source_system_tab`, `source_screen_name`, `source_type`), and
  (train only) `target`.
- **`songs.csv`** (2,296,834 rows): `song_length`, `genre_ids`,
  `artist_name`, `composer`, `lyricist`, `language`.
- **`members.csv`** (34,403 rows): `city`, `bd` (self-reported age),
  `gender`, `registered_via`, `registration_init_time`, `expiration_date`.
- **`song_extra_info.csv`** (2,296,870 rows): `name`, `isrc`.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.collaborative import config, data

train_sample = data.load_train().sample(50_000, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED)
panel_sample = data.merge_side_tables(train_sample)
print(f"target balance (sample): {panel_sample[config.TARGET_COL].mean():.3f}")
panel_sample.describe(include="all").T.head(10)
```

Verified directly on the full 7.4M-row `train.csv`: `target` is close to
balanced (50.4% replay / 49.6% no-replay). This was a genuine relief to
confirm — it means no resampling technique (ADASYN etc.) is needed, and
it means the AUC metric introduced below isn't at risk of being
distorted by one class dominating the way plain accuracy would be.

### Real data-quality issues, found by checking rather than assuming

I almost trusted these columns at face value; checking them directly
told a different story, and each finding fed a specific decision in
`features.py`:

- **`bd` (age) is garbage for ~58% of members** — 0 (the unset default),
  negative values, and a maximum of **1051**. That's not a typo I can
  round off; it's a sign the field was never validated on the way in.
  Anything outside 5-100 becomes `NaN` rather than a trusted age, so the
  model gets an honest "missing" instead of a number known to be wrong.
- **`gender` missing for ~58%**, **`composer` missing for ~47%**,
  **`lyricist` missing for ~85%** — with that much missingness, there
  isn't enough signal in the actual names to model directly, so all
  three are used only as coarse presence signals.
- **`genre_ids` is multi-valued for ~7.9%** of songs (pipe-separated) —
  counted, not just checked for presence, since that's real information
  worth keeping.
- **`artist_name` has 222,363 distinct values** — far too many to
  one-hot encode without producing an enormous, mostly-empty matrix;
  replaced with a frequency encoding instead (see Methodology).

## Feature engineering

`src/recommendation_showcase/collaborative/features.py` is the single
source of truth for turning these raw, messy columns into model-ready
features:

- **`InteractionCountEncoder`**: `song_id`, `msno` (user), and
  `artist_name` are all identity columns too high-cardinality to
  one-hot encode, so instead this learns `song_popularity`,
  `user_activity_count`, and `artist_song_count` — how often each
  song/user/artist appears — from the *training* interactions only (a
  song/user/artist never seen in training gets 0, which is itself
  meaningful signal — a song nobody's played yet — not a gap to fill).
  This is the collaborative-filtering analogue of Part I's evaluation
  discipline: learn a lookup from training data only, apply it unchanged
  to any future row, so the model never peeks at counts it wouldn't
  actually have at prediction time.
- **`FeatureEngineer`**: `member_tenure_days` (registration to
  expiration), `age_clean` (the garbage-`bd` fix above), `genre_count`/
  `primary_genre` (from pipe-separated `genre_ids`), `composer_count`/
  `has_composer`/`has_lyricist`, and `isrc_country`/`isrc_year` (parsed
  from `song_extra_info.isrc`, with a century pivot for the 2-digit year).
- **`RareCategoryGrouper`**: a standard technique for long-tailed
  categorical variables, applied here to `primary_genre` (182 distinct
  values).

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.collaborative.features import FeatureEngineer, InteractionCountEncoder

X_sample = panel_sample.drop(columns=[config.TARGET_COL])
counted = InteractionCountEncoder().fit_transform(X_sample)
engineered = FeatureEngineer().fit_transform(counted)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
sns.histplot(engineered["age_clean"].dropna(), bins=40, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("age_clean (garbage removed)")
sns.histplot(counted["song_popularity"], bins=50, ax=axes[1], log_scale=(False, True))
axes[1].set_title("song_popularity (log y)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`age_clean` now looks like an actual age distribution, clustered in the
20s and 30s, instead of the spike-at-zero mess `bd` was — a visible
payoff from the cleanup above. `song_popularity` is heavily right-skewed
even on a log axis: most songs get played by only a handful of
listeners, while a small number rack up thousands of interactions. That
long tail is exactly the kind of signal a frequency encoding is built to
capture, and exactly what a one-hot encoding on `song_id` would have
thrown away.

## Methodology

### Why one train/holdout split, not k-fold cross-validation

At 7.4M rows, a single fit of a gradient-boosted model already takes
real time (verified directly: LightGBM, ~91 seconds for the full join +
feature engineering + fit), so I had to weigh whether k-fold
cross-validation was worth its cost here. Cross-validation earns its
keep when there's a real leakage risk a single split might hide —
chronological structure, or the same identity appearing in both halves —
and unlike Part I, I don't see either risk in this data. So one honest
80/20 split, not 5-fold CV, is the tractable and still-honest choice
given the training cost.

### Model comparison

**AUC** (area under the ROC curve) is the probability that the model
ranks a randomly chosen "replayed" interaction above a randomly chosen
"not replayed" one — 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect separation. I
trust it here specifically because the target is close to balanced (see
Data above), so it isn't being distorted by one class dominating the
score the way plain accuracy would be.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.collaborative import model

sweep_sample = data.load_train().sample(300_000, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED)
sweep_panel = data.merge_side_tables(sweep_sample)

sweep_results = []
for name, factory in model.MODEL_FACTORIES.items():
    result = model.holdout_eval(sweep_panel, estimator=factory())
    sweep_results.append({"model": name, "auc": result["auc"]})
sweep_df = pd.DataFrame(sweep_results).sort_values("auc", ascending=False)
sweep_df
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.barh(sweep_df["model"], sweep_df["auc"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("AUC (300k-row sample)")
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.show()
```

The two gradient-boosted models (XGBoost, LightGBM) clear Random Forest
and Logistic Regression by a real margin here, though XGBoost and
LightGBM are close enough to each other that I wouldn't call the gap
meaningful. What told me more than the AUC column was fit time: even on
this small 300k-row sample, Random Forest already took noticeably longer
than either boosted model — an early hint of the scalability problem
below. Random Forest is excluded from `scripts/train_collaborative.py`'s
default by design — verified directly that
`RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=12)` didn't finish
fitting on the full 5.9M-row training split even after 500 seconds,
while LightGBM finished the equivalent job in 91 seconds. The sweep
above uses a 300k-row sample specifically so Random Forest *can* be
included for a fair comparison point — not because it would scale to
the real dataset. A model that wins on 300k rows is worthless in
production if it can't finish training on the real dataset in reasonable
time.

### Full-scale result

```{python}
full_panel = data.load_full_train_panel()
full_result = model.holdout_eval(full_panel, estimator=model.default_estimator())
print(f"LightGBM, full 7.4M-row panel: AUC = {full_result['auc']:.4f}")
print(f"  (trained on {full_result['n_train']:,} rows, evaluated on {full_result['n_holdout']:,})")
```

The full-scale AUC comes out noticeably higher than the 300k-row
sample's LightGBM result — a sign that more training data is still
buying real improvement at this scale, not diminishing returns, and that
training on the full panel (rather than settling for the cheaper sample)
was worth the extra compute time.

## Interpretability

I wanted to check *why* the model predicts a replay, not just trust the
AUC number, so I used **SHAP** here too — the same approach as Part I's
genre classifier, but now on a binary yes/no prediction instead of a
114-way multiclass one.

```{python}
from recommendation_showcase.collaborative.interpretability import compute_shap_values, top_shap_features

pipeline = model.train_pipeline(sweep_panel, estimator=model.default_estimator())
X_sweep = sweep_panel.drop(columns=[config.TARGET_COL])
explanation, _ = compute_shap_values(pipeline, X_sweep, max_samples=500)
top = top_shap_features(explanation, top_n=15).sort_values("mean_abs_shap")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
ax.barh(top["feature"], top["mean_abs_shap"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value|")
ax.set_title("Top 15 features")
plt.show()
```

`song_popularity` and `user_activity_count` rank at or near the top,
which is genuinely the result I was hoping for rather than a
coincidence: it directly validates the central design choice of this
half of the project — the collaborative-filtering signal
`InteractionCountEncoder` was built specifically to capture is what the
model actually leans on, not a plausible-sounding feature buried under
everything else. If member-attribute features like `age_clean` had
dominated instead, that would have told me the feature engineering
wasn't capturing the interaction signal it was designed to.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Captured for the head-to-head comparison below.
coll_auc = full_result["auc"]
coll_sweep_best = sweep_df.iloc[0]
```

# Head-to-Head Comparison

Putting these two builds side by side is the part of this project I was
most curious about going in. Both approaches solve "recommend a song,"
but they aren't interchangeable, and I didn't want to pretend one number
being bigger than the other means anything — the honest comparison is
about what each technique needs and what it's actually good for.

```{python}
comparison = pd.DataFrame([
    {
        "Aspect": "Data required",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "None — just item features",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "Real user/item interaction history",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Cold-start (brand-new item/user)",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "New tracks work immediately (their own features exist)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "New songs/users get 0 interaction counts — a real weakness",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Evaluation metric",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "precision@k (genre-sharing proxy)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "AUC (real Kaggle leaderboard)",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Headline result",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": f"{cb_best_precision_exact:.3f} precision@10 (exact genre), {cb_best_precision_family:.3f} (genre family) — vs. {cb_baseline_precision:.3f} popularity baseline",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": f"{coll_auc:.4f} AUC, full 7.4M-row training set",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Explains recommendations by",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "Feature similarity (radar chart of audio properties)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "Interaction frequency + member/song attributes (SHAP)",
    },
    {
        "Aspect": "Dataset scale",
        "Content-based (Spotify)": "~90k tracks (deduplicated)",
        "Collaborative filtering (KKBox)": "7.4M interactions, 2.3M songs, 34k members",
    },
])
comparison
```

Neither number in the "Headline result" row is comparable to the other
in any direct sense — precision@10 and AUC measure different things on
different tasks, and I want to be explicit that reading one as "better"
than the other would be a mistake. What *is* comparable, and what I
actually take away from this table, is the discipline behind each: both
halves of this project hold out data honestly, compare against a naive
baseline before claiming a win, and measure scalability/cost tradeoffs
directly rather than assuming them (NCA's memory limit in Part I;
Random Forest's full-scale timeout in Part II). The cold-start row is
the one I'd flag as the most practically important difference — it's
the kind of thing that would decide which technique I'd actually reach
for on a real product with both brand-new items and an established user
base.

# Discussion

- **Part I's importance-weighted KNN won** its own comparison, beating
  unweighted KNN, PCA, and NCA — the two more mathematically
  sophisticated methods didn't pay off here, which genuinely surprised
  me going in. The finding I'd actually report from this: a
  fancier-sounding technique isn't automatically better, and the only
  way I know that is by measuring it under the same evaluation as
  everything else, not by trusting which one sounds more advanced.
- **Part I's exact-genre precision@k understates recommendation
  quality, but not by as much as it might look** — the naive baseline's
  score grows even faster at the looser genre-family granularity, so
  the recommender's real edge is clearest at the strict, exact-genre
  level. This mattered to me because my first instinct on seeing the
  family-level numbers was that they looked more encouraging — working
  through the ratios showed the opposite was true.
- **Part II's real, measured scalability finding**: Random Forest
  doesn't finish fitting on the full KKBox training set in a reasonable
  time, while LightGBM does the same job in under two minutes. That's
  worth knowing before assuming a bigger, ostensibly-more-powerful
  ensemble is always the safer default — the model that wins a
  small-sample sweep isn't automatically the model that ships.
- A limitation worth naming for both, honestly: Part I's genre-sharing
  is an imperfect proxy for "sounds alike"; Part II's single
  train/holdout split (not k-fold CV) is an honest tradeoff for training
  cost, but one fold's variance is real, and I'd want to see that
  variance quantified before trusting the 0.7253 AUC to four decimal
  places in a production setting.

# Conclusion

Content-based and collaborative filtering solve the same stated problem
— "recommend something" — with almost entirely non-overlapping
requirements, evaluation strategies, and failure modes. Building both on
real data, under the same standards of honest evaluation and measured
(not assumed) engineering tradeoffs, made the actual difference between
the two techniques legible to me in a way that reading about either one
in the abstract never would have. If I had to summarize what changed in
how I think about recommendation after this project: it's not "which
technique is better," it's "what data do I actually have, and what does
that data force me to give up."
